adults.title: The Person in Front of You
adults.big_idea: We keep the covenant we renew at the sacrament by ministering with compassion to whomever God places in our path.
adults.objective: Learners will connect their sacrament covenant to everyday ministering and choose one way to pray for, notice and act on a divine appointment this week.
prepare: Read President Farnes’s talk, “Divine Appointments,” especially paragraphs T10.10–T10.23 and T10.38–T10.39.
Bring a slip of paper and a pen for each person.
Write three words on the board before class: SEE, FEEL, ACT.
Ask one person ahead of time to be ready to read the Elder Oaks story aloud (T10.06–T10.16).

segments.name: Someone who noticed
steps: After the prayer, ask everyone to think silently for 30 seconds about a time when someone noticed them on a hard day, perhaps with only a question or a few kind words.
Invite them to turn to a neighbor and share for one minute each. Ask them to listen for what the other person actually did.
Take two or three short responses to the question below. Write the small actions on the board (asked, waited, listened, sat with me).
questions: What did that person do that made the difference? How big was it, really?

segments.name: It’s what we do
steps: Explain that President Farnes, Young Men General President, told of a discouraging Saturday almost 20 years ago when he was serving as a bishop and had just been called into a stake presidency. He went to a ward temple night without the best attitude.
Have your reader read T10.06–T10.16 aloud. In the story, President Oaks was then Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles.
Ask the class to name everything Elder Oaks did. List it under the words on the board: he asked, he waited, he asked again, he listened, he thanked, he encouraged, he embraced.
Point out that five years later Elder Oaks did not remember the conversation. Read his reply once more: “But it’s what we do. Isn’t it?”
Discuss the questions. Let several people answer before you add anything.
questions: Brother Farnes first answered that everything was great. What helped him open up the second time?
What does it tell you that Elder Oaks did not remember a moment that changed another man’s life?

segments.name: A covenant of compassion
steps: Invite everyone to open to Moroni 4:3 and read it silently, looking for what we tell Heavenly Father we are willing to do and what He promises in return.
Read aloud the key quote from T10.17 about what it means to take His name upon us. Then read T10.19, the paragraph where President Farnes names these moments “divine appointments.”

Give two minutes of silent writing on the slip of paper: When someone encounters me on an ordinary Tuesday, what of Jesus Christ do they experience? Which of the five (kindness, patience, hope, love, compassion) do I most want to grow in?
Invite one or two people to share a thought, only if they wish. Do not ask anyone to read what they wrote.
questions: How does it change ministering to think of it as a way we keep the sacrament covenant, every day, and not only as an assignment?

segments.name: Eyes to see
steps: Divide into groups of three or four. Ask each group to read Luke 10:30–35 and mark where the Samaritan sees, where he feels and where he acts. Give three minutes.
Bring the class back. Read T10.20–T10.21 and point to the three words on the board.

Briefly retell the airport story (T10.24–T10.38): President Farnes had earbuds in and a book open when he noticed a frightened young missionary in tears. He went back to his book. The Spirit prompted him to look again. He and his wife, Linsey, helped the elder board, the only empty seat turned out to be next to President Farnes, and at the baggage claim the elder hugged them before he greeted his mission leaders.
Read the aligned quote from President Spencer W. Kimball, which President Eyring shared at this conference. Then ask the questions.
questions: President Farnes said he was embarrassed by how slow he had been to help. What are the earbuds and the book in your life, the ordinary things that keep you from looking up?
When has someone who first looked like an interruption turned out to be the reason you were there?

segments.name: Pray, see, act
steps: Read both invitations from T10.39 aloud. Point out the promise that goes with them: the Lord promises that we can always have His Spirit with us, and with that gift we can minister as the Savior would (T10.18). President Farnes also taught that when we use the eyes God has given us, we begin to recognize divine appointments all around us (T10.22).

Ask each person to turn the slip of paper over and finish two lines: This week I will pray for eyes to see at this time of day. One place I will look up is here (the hallway at church, the break room, the school pickup line, my own kitchen).
Check for understanding: ask one person to say the pattern in their own words, from sacrament covenant to the person in front of them.
Tell the class that next week you will begin by asking who had a divine appointment, and whether they were the one who helped or the one who was helped.
Close with your own short testimony that the Savior sees each person in the room, and that He will help them see.

key_quotes.text: As covenant followers of Jesus Christ, we minister with compassion to whomever God places in our path.
It means that when someone encounters us, they should experience something of Jesus Christ—His kindness, His patience, His hope, His love, His compassion.
To Jesus, these people were not interrupting His mission. They were His mission.
All we had to do was see the person God had placed in our path, look with compassion rather than judgment, and then act.

scriptures.use: Read silently in segment 3. Look for what we witness we are willing to do and what the Lord promises in return.
Read in groups of three or four in segment 4. Mark where the Samaritan sees, feels and acts.
Offer as home study for the week: read it after praying for eyes to see, and ask whom the Savior counts our small acts as done for.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Spencer W. Kimball, quoted by President Eyring
aligned_quotes.text: God does notice us, and he watches over us. But it is usually through another person that he meets our needs.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Sinclair
aligned_quotes.text: a true disciple of Jesus Christ is quick to help and slow to judge

invitations.text: let us pray every day for eyes to see the divine appointments God places before us!
Let us put compassion into action and minister to the person in front of us.

takeaways: At the sacrament I promise to take the Savior’s name upon me; I keep that promise with the people I meet every day.
People are not interruptions to my discipleship. They are my discipleship.
I can pray for eyes to see, look with compassion rather than judgment, and then act.
act: Each morning this week, pray by name for eyes to see the person God places in your path that day.
Choose one place where you usually look down (a waiting room, a hallway, the foyer) and look up there on purpose.
When someone answers that they are fine, and you sense they are not, ask a second time, gently, and listen.
During the sacrament next Sunday, think of one person you met this week and ask what the Savior would have you do next.
adapt: At home or with two or three people: skip the groups. Read Luke 10:30–35 together, then let each person tell about someone who noticed them.
Large class: do every discussion in pairs first, then take only two responses from the whole room so the timing holds.
Short on time: keep segments 2, 3 and 5. Retell the airport story in three sentences during the closing.

youth.title: Look Again
youth.big_idea: Because we have promised to follow Jesus Christ, we look for the person God places in our path and help them, the way the Savior would.
youth.objective: Youth will be able to explain the pattern of seeing, feeling compassion and acting, and will choose one place this week where they will look up and help someone.
prepare: Read President Farnes’s talk, “Divine Appointments.” Know the airport story (T10.24–T10.38) well enough to tell it.
Bring paper and pens for teams, and a timer (a phone works).
Write on the board: SEE → FEEL → ACT.
Ask the youth to have their scriptures or the Gospel Library app ready.

segments.name: Looking is not seeing
steps: Start right away. Put the youth in pairs, facing each other, and give them 15 seconds to look at their partner without talking.

Have them turn back to back. Ask three quick questions each person answers quietly to their partner: What color are your partner’s shoes? Is your partner wearing a watch or a bracelet? What is in your partner’s hands?
Let them turn around and check. Enjoy the laughter, then ask the question below and take two answers.
questions: You were looking straight at them. Why did you miss it?

segments.name: The missionary with the alarm clock
steps: Explain that President Farnes, the Young Men General President, told of waiting at an airport with his wife, Linsey, with his earbuds in and a book open.
Have three youth read T10.25, T10.26 and T10.27 aloud from their phones, one paragraph each. Stop after the first sentence of T10.26, where he goes back to his book, and ask the first question.

Finish T10.26–T10.27, then tell the rest in your own words: the elder was far from his home country, alone on a plane for the first time, and holding the clock so he would not miss the flight. President and Sister Farnes walked him to the gate. He was the last to board, and the only empty seat was next to President Farnes. When they landed, they walked him arm in arm to the baggage claim, and he hugged them before he greeted his mission leaders.
Ask the second question.
questions: Be honest: why is it so easy to look back down at the book, or the phone?
What made the difference between the first look and the second?

segments.name: Find the pattern
steps: Make teams of two or three. Give each team paper and a pen.
Challenge: read Luke 10:30–35 and list every single thing the Samaritan did for the wounded traveler. Three minutes on the timer. The team with the longest accurate list wins.
Have the winning team read their list. Then ask every team to circle the one action that had to come first.
Read T10.20 aloud, beginning where President Farnes says others saw an inconvenience or an interruption. Point to the board: see, feel, act.
questions: The others on that road saw the same man. What did the Samaritan see that they did not?

segments.name: Why we do this
steps: Ask the youth to open to D&C 20:77 and find two things: what we tell Heavenly Father we are willing to do, and what He promises us. Take answers.
Read the key quote from T10.17 about what it means to take the Savior’s name upon us.

Tell the first story briefly: years ago, when President Farnes was a discouraged bishop, President Oaks (then Elder Dallin H. Oaks) stopped him in the temple, waited for him, and said, “Brother, tell me how you are really doing.” Five years later Elder Oaks did not remember it. He said, “But it’s what we do. Isn’t it?”
Ask the question below. Give them ten seconds of quiet before anyone answers.
questions: If someone ran into you at school this week, what of Jesus Christ would they experience?

segments.name: Thirty-second rescues
steps: Keep the same teams. Give each team one made-up situation: (1) someone new is eating alone at lunch; (2) a friend who is usually loud in the group chat has gone silent for three days; (3) a younger child at a Church activity is standing by the wall; (4) a teammate walks off after a bad game without talking to anyone.
Each team has two minutes to plan a 30-second role play that shows all three steps: what they would notice, what the other person might be feeling, and one thing they would actually say or do.
Watch each role play. After each one, have the class name the see, the feel and the act.
Read President Chibota’s aligned quote about learning a name. Then raise the honest worries below and let the youth answer each other.
questions: What if it is awkward, or they do not want help?
President Farnes almost missed it and felt embarrassed. What does it mean to you that the Spirit prompted him to look again?

segments.name: This week’s challenge
steps: Read both invitations from T10.39. Share the promise: the Lord promises that we can always have His Spirit with us, and with that gift we can minister as the Savior would (T10.18).
Challenge: for seven days, pray each morning for eyes to see. Pick one place where you will take the earbuds out and look up (the bus, the hallway, lunch, the foyer). Help one person.
Have each youth type the place into a note on their phone, or write it on paper, and finish this line: This week I will look up at…
Check for understanding: ask one youth to explain see, feel, act to the class in one sentence.
Tell them next week begins with two minutes of reports: who did you see? Bear a brief testimony that the Savior sees each of them.

key_quotes.text: Seeing awakened compassion. Compassion moved him to act. And his actions changed a life forever.
That means we choose to see as He sees, feel as He feels, and do as He would do.
But the Spirit prompted me to look again.
What once looked like random encounters become invitations from the Lord to minister with compassion.

scriptures.use: Team challenge in segment 3: list everything the Samaritan did, then circle what had to come first.
Read in segment 4. Find what we say we are willing to do and what Heavenly Father promises us.
Optional memory verse for the week: read it together at the close and ask whom we are really serving when we help the person in front of us.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Chibota
aligned_quotes.text: Often, helping others feel seen as children of God begins with something as simple as learning their name.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Sinclair
aligned_quotes.text: a true disciple of Jesus Christ is quick to help and slow to judge

invitations.text: let us pray every day for eyes to see the divine appointments God places before us!
Let us put compassion into action and minister to the person in front of us.

takeaways: When I take the sacrament, I promise to see, feel and do as the Savior would.
The people around me are not random. Some of them are invitations from the Lord.
If I miss it the first time, the Spirit can prompt me to look again.
act: Pray every morning for seven days for eyes to see who needs you that day.
Choose one place to take your earbuds out and look up, and stick with it all week.
Learn the name of one person you see often but have never spoken to, and use it.
When you notice someone and feel that small nudge, act within a minute, before you talk yourself out of it.
adapt: At home or with one or two youth: do the Luke 10 list together against the timer, and talk through one situation in place of the role plays.
Large class: run the role plays in two halves of the room at once and have each half pick one to show everyone.
Short on time: keep segments 1, 2 and 6, and read the T10.20 quote as you point to the board.

children.title: Eyes to See and Hands to Help
children.big_idea: Heavenly Father helps me see people who need help, and I can help them like Jesus did.
children.objective: Children will be able to say and act out three steps (I see, I care, I help) and will choose one person they can help this week.
prepare: Read the airport story in President Farnes’s talk (T10.24–T10.38) so you can tell it simply in your own words.
Bring a flashlight, a small blanket, paper and crayons.
Before class, draw four simple faces on separate papers (sad, worried, lonely, tired) and place them around the room where children can find them.
Bring one extra sheet of paper to be a pretend ticket and a block or small box to be a pretend clock.

segments.name: Looking eyes
steps: Greet each child by name. Sing the first verse of the song I’m Trying to Be like Jesus together.
Show the children how to make pretend glasses by curling their fingers around their eyes. Ask them to look around the room and find something blue, then something round, then a friend who is smiling.

Tell them: today we will learn that Heavenly Father helps us see people who need help. Teach the three steps with actions: I see (hands around eyes), I care (hands on heart), I help (hands held out). Say it together twice.

segments.name: The missionary at the airport
steps: Explain that President Farnes, a leader in the Church, told a true story in general conference. Invite one child to be the missionary and hold the paper ticket and the pretend clock. Invite two children to be President Farnes and his wife, Sister Farnes.

Tell the story simply while the children act it out. A young missionary sat at the airport. He was far from home, he had never been on an airplane alone, and he was scared. He held a clock so he would not miss his plane. President Farnes was reading a book. He looked up and then looked back down at his book.
Pause and ask the first question. Then go on: the Holy Ghost helped President Farnes look again. He asked the missionary if he was OK. He and Sister Farnes showed him where to go.
Have all the children line up as the airplane. The missionary gets on last and finds the only empty seat, right next to President Farnes. Let the missionary pretend to fall asleep.

Finish: when the plane landed, they walked with him, arm in arm, until he found his mission leaders. He was so thankful that he gave them a big hug. Do the three actions together: I see, I care, I help.
questions: How do you think the missionary felt?
Who helped President Farnes look again?

segments.name: Jesus told a story
steps: Hold up the scriptures and say that Jesus told a story about a man with eyes to see. It is in Luke 10:30–35.
Lay the blanket on the floor as the road. Invite one child to sit on the blanket as the traveler who was hurt and needed help.
Have the other children walk past on the far side of the room, looking away. Then have them walk again, and this time stop, kneel down, and gently place the blanket around the traveler’s shoulders.
Help the traveler stand and walk together to the inn (a chair). Trade places and do it once more if time allows.
Ask the question, then do the three actions again.
questions: Which helper was like Jesus? What did he do first?

segments.name: The helping light
steps: Gather the children in a circle and hold up the flashlight. Say: when we pray, Heavenly Father can help us notice people who need us. Let’s practice noticing.
Give one child the flashlight and ask them to shine it around the room until they find one of the paper faces. Keep the room lights on so everyone feels safe.
When the light lands on a face, ask the class how that person might feel and one thing we could do to help (sit by them, say hello, share, get a grown-up, smile).
Pass the flashlight to another child and repeat until all four faces are found.
questions: How do you think this person feels?
What could we do to help?

segments.name: Draw someone I can help
steps: Give each child paper and crayons. Ask them to draw two big circles like a pair of glasses.
Inside the glasses, have them draw someone they could help this week and what they will do. It can be anyone: someone at home, at school, at church or in their neighborhood.
Walk around and ask each child to tell you about the drawing. Write a few words under the picture for the younger children.
Invite two or three children to show their drawing and say who they will help.

segments.name: Pray for eyes to see
steps: Tell the children that President Farnes invited everyone to pray every day for eyes to see the people Heavenly Father places in front of us, and then to help them.
Teach one sentence they can add to their prayers: Heavenly Father, please help me see someone I can help today. Say it together, phrase by phrase, two times.
Check for understanding: ask the children to show you the three steps with actions and no words, then say them aloud.
Tell them that next week you will ask who they helped. Ask them to put the drawing where they will see it at home.

segments.name: Closing song and testimony
steps: Sing “Kindness Begins with Me.”
Bear a short testimony: Jesus sees each one of you. He loves you. He will help you see people who need help.
Invite a child to give the closing prayer and, if they wish, to use the sentence you practiced.

key_quotes.text: God has given us eyes to see.
It’s what Jesus did. And it’s what we do.
But the Spirit prompted me to look again.

scriptures.use: Show the children where the story is, then act it out with the blanket in segment 3. An older child may read verses 33–34 aloud.
For ages 8–11: have a child read it aloud after the drawing activity and ask who we are also serving when we help someone.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Rasband
aligned_quotes.text: Love is being there with arms outstretched and a cheerful countenance.

invitations.text: let us pray every day for eyes to see the divine appointments God places before us!
Let us put compassion into action and minister to the person in front of us.

takeaways: Heavenly Father helps me see people who need help.
I see, I care, I help.
When I help someone, I am being like Jesus.
act: Ask Heavenly Father in your prayers each day to help you see someone you can help.
Help the person in your drawing this week.
When you see someone alone or sad, say hello and smile.
music: I'm Trying to Be like Jesus

adapt.younger: For ages 3–7: keep the two stories very short and let every child have a turn as a helper. Repeat the three actions (I see, I care, I help) after every activity. Skip writing; ask each child to tell you about the drawing. If they are restless, shorten the flashlight activity to two faces and sing the opening song again with actions.
adapt.older: For ages 8–11: let an older child read Luke 10:33–34 aloud and another lead the flashlight activity. Read Elder Rasband’s aligned quote and ask what arms outstretched could look like at school. Ask a harder question: why is it sometimes easier to look away, and what can we do when we feel that? Have them read Mosiah 2:17 and write one sentence under their drawing about what they will do.
